speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Miss Carney that Bill C-94, an Act to implement an agreement between the Government of Canada and the Government of Newfoundland and Labrador on offshore petroleum resource management and revenue sharing and to make related and consequential amendments, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe):
subtopic: CANADA-NEWFOUNDLAND ATLANTIC ACCORD IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in debate on Bill C-94, particularly because I have the opportunity to rise following the Hon. Member for Bonavista-Trinity-Conception (Mr. Johnson), unfortunately interrupted by lunch hour and Question Period.
The Hon. Member told the House a few hours ago that the Atlantic Accord represented a panacea for all of Newfoundland's problems. He said that with the historic Atlantic Accord, Newfoundland would finally mature and come into its own in Confederation and countless jobs and billions of dollars would flow to the Province of Newfoundland.
I say that I am pleased to speak following the Hon. Member for two reasons. The first is that it was interesting to listen to him and to understand the extent of the enthusiasm of Conservative Members and the extent to which they will go to try to rationalize this incredible package that was put together by the federal Government and the Government of Newfoundland.
All Members of Parliament will recall that a few short years ago the Premier of Newfoundland, Brian Peckford, was very vocal in putting forward Newfoundland's offshore position when a Party of another stripe was in power. He travelled the country, toured the land. He made himself available to the national press and he laid down Newfoundland's position.
Let us examine the position Mr. Peckford put to the previous Liberal administration, a position to which he required agreement or he would not sign a deal, as compared to what is contained in Bill C-94. That will be an interesting
exercise. Let us see what the Premier got from this Government that he could not get from the previous Government, and let us see how consistent the Premier has been.
First we all recall that the Premier of Newfoundland said when it came to the offshore Newfoundland that his first requirement for signing an agreement with Ottawa would be that Newfoundland's ownership of the resource be recognized explicitly. Not only must Newfoundland's ownership of the resource be recognized explicitly, but it must be entrenched in the Constitution, never to be challenged again. That was the position taken by the Premier at that time. What did he receive in this document that he subsequently signed? The document recognizes that the offshore belongs to all the people of Canada, not to Newfoundland. That had been condition number one.
The Premier's condition number two, logical man that he is, was that if Newfoundlanders own the offshore, 100 per cent of the revenues that flow from it should go to Newfoundland. That was a logical step for the Premier to take having declared ownership of the resource. What did he get in this agreement that he signed with the current Government? Did he get 100 per cent of revenues? He was promised 50 per cent of the revenues from the back-in provision but the back-in provision on Canada lands has since been cancelled. He got 50 per cent of nothing. On the revenue-sharing agreement, we still do not know what the revenues will be, or if there are to be any at all given the current state of the offshore. That was condition number two.
The third thing the Premier said was that the offshore is very important to Newfoundland. He went on to say that Newfoundland was terrified of the fantastic and incredible impact of rapid development, that it could not handle the billions of dollars that would flood the province, and that it could not handle the number of jobs that would be created. He said that Newfoundland wanted to control the pace of development in that province, and that he did not want the economy to heat up too quickly. He felt that with 29 per cent unemployment, Newfoundland did not want too much development at too fast a pace. Therefore Newfoundland would insist that it control the pace of development.
What did Newfoundland receive from this agreement, from Premier Peckford and his buddy of the same blue stripe? It was a blue day when the agreement was signed. Newfoundland did not get control over the pace of development. It got Clause 35(2) which guarantees that Ottawa or the Minister of Energy shall control the pace of development. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) will determine whether Canada's security of supply has been met for a period of five years. That is contained in Bill C-94.
What else did the Premier of Newfoundland demand as part of the agreement with the previous Liberal Government? He demanded that Hibernia crude oil be used in processing facilities in Newfoundland, and that the raw resource should
May 26, 1986

be used to create a petrochemical industry in that province. He said that it must be part of the agreement. However, what did he sign with the Government of today? He signed Clause 41 which includes a guarantee of supply for a plant called Come-By-Chance that has been closed for the last 10 years. How valuable an asset is the Come-By-Chance plant to which the Government of Canada was to supply Hibernia crude? It was so valuable that the President of Petro-Canada said that he would sell it for a dollar if he could find a buyer! We know that the plant will not use Hibernia crude.
What did the agreement indicate about the possibility of developing new or additional facilities to become involved in the petrochemical industry some time down the road, perhaps in five years or twenty-five years? It indicates that it could only happen when the existing capacity and needs of all other plants in Atlantic Canada have been met. There is no security of supply for Newfoundland in Bill C-94.
I agree and have always agreed with the principle that offshore resources belong to the entire country. That was the Liberal position. Because of where the resource is located, the benefits from offshore should first flow to Newfoundland and Newfoundlanders. That was also our position. The resource should be jointly managed and controlled for the benefit of the country and the benefit of the province. That was our position as well.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subtopic: CANADA-NEWFOUNDLAND ATLANTIC ACCORD IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Why didn't you bring in a deal?

subtopic: CANADA-NEWFOUNDLAND ATLANTIC ACCORD IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Because Mr. Peckford was incapable of signing a reasonable deal. When he was in political trouble he got himself into a position where he had to tell Newfoundlanders, "Let us re-elect Brian Peckford because Brian Peckford can sign a deal with Brian Mulroney". The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) made sure that he put a deal to Mr. Peckford a month before the provincial election. Mr. Peckford, knowing that he dare not go into a provincial election without some kind of agreement, took anything he could get, and what he got was absolutely nothing.
How do we examine Bill C-94? Do we examine it in relation to the current oil patch? Do we examine it in terms of the reality that the projected investment in the oil patch for this year has dropped from $11.2 billion down to $6 billion, or nearly a 50 per cent reduction? Do we examine it in face of the fact that job projections now indicate that 4,000 jobs will be lost in that industry in 1986? Do we examine it in face of the fact that where we once had 14 rigs operating on the East Coast in the offshore, we now have only six? Do we examine it in the context of the industry five months or six months ago when the world price of oil was double what it is now? If we examine Bill C-94 in the face of current reality versus the euphoric mood in which it was written, we discover that it is no longer relevant. Bill C-94 is irrelevant.
A few days ago in the House we dealt with second reading stage of Bill C-92, an Act to set up a tax credit scheme for exploration off the East Coast of Canada in the offshore. It replaced PIP, under which Canadian companies operating in
Atlantic Accord
the offshore received more than $40 million worth of assistance for every $50 million worth of high risk frontier exploration. What has replaced that program? It has been replaced by a new tax credit scheme. In place of $40 million worth of tax credit for $50 million worth of expenditure, $4.5 million will be given. That is a loss of some $35 million on a $50 million per unit exploration program.
In its haste to respond to American demands that Canada's oil patch be passed back to the corporate boardrooms of the United States, the Government of Canada gutted the National Energy Program. It did not review, retool, or fine tune it to make it more relevant to changing conditions. Instead it gutted the program. It got rid of the Canadian ownership aspect of the program, the incentives to ensure exploration in the High Arctic, in the Beaufort Sea, off Sable Island, Nova Scotia, off Labrador, at Ben Nevis, and in Hibernia. That is what the Government did. It removed Canadian oil companies which were becoming a window on an industry vital to the country, an industry that provides the fuel which drives the engine of our economy. It removed those Canadian interests and put corporate planning and policy-making back into the hands of those people who sit in boardrooms in glass and steel towers outside Canada.
What do those people who sit in boardrooms in glass towers outside the country say about the Hibernia development, the tar sands in Alberta, the Beaufort Sea, or the area of nonconventional oil exploration? They are saying, "there is not a quick buck to be made and we are out of it". What are they saying about Canadian security of supply, having resources at our disposal to ensure that never again are we victims held hostage by OPEC? They are saying, "there is not a quick buck to be made and we are out of it".
What about Canadian citizens owning a piece of a Canadian resource and Canadian content in the oil and gas industry? Those same people are saying that the companies are now going into bankruptcy because of the policies of the Government of Canada, that they are in big trouble with their banks, and that they can buy them cheap. That is the kind of shortsighted, doctrinaire, market-place philosophy which the Government has followed.
No one is rejoicing the passage of the Atlantic Accord in Newfoundland today. I call it the "Atlantic squeeze". The Premier of Newfoundland will not even bring in the parallel legislation which is to be passed in the Newfoundland Legislature. He had two days or three days of debate on it, and he got such heat in the legislature and such negative press that he pulled it back out again. The great Atlantic Accord is being treated like a pea in a series of cups. No one knows when the correct cup will come up and the Atlantic Accord will reappear in all its finery.
The people of Newfoundland are feeling a sense of lost opportunity about the Newfoundland offshore. They are almost feeling the sense of a death in the family. However, no one has yet declared that the patient has died and that the funeral date has been set. Because of the narrow, parochial,

May 26, 1986
Atlantic Accord
political position of the Premier of Newfoundland, who wasted an opportunity to move forward with development, Hibernia is not going today. In 1986 we live in a dramatically different world from the world in which we lived twenty weeks ago, two years ago, or five years ago. We now have a world price for oil, in the current fiscal regime set up by the Conservative Government, where Hibernia is not going. We are faced with losing a tremendous number of skilled people, individuals who have been drawn from all across the country, many from my own province, highly skilled, highly trained in the oil and gas industry. We are faced with losing those people across the face of the earth. That pool of talent is being dissipated because the Government has decided that it is the corporate boardrooms south of the border rather than the needs of Canadians that will determine energy policy in Canada.
We in Newfoundland who had but a thread of a dream, who had but a thread of the possibility that revenues from oil and gas could do for our province, perhaps empathize more than anybody else with what is happening in Alberta. That is a province that was using oil and gas revenue to build on other sectors in Alberta, using non-renewable resource revenues to build on traditional revenues for traditional resources, but is now facing an economy in shambles, and is confronted with a Government that says, "I am sorry, the philosophy of the day says that the market shall dictate whether or not you work, my friend. The philosophy of the day says OPEC's manipulations shall decide whether you pay the mortgage, my friend. The philosophy of the day says your future and Canada's oil and gas industry shall have its agenda decided south of the border or in the Middle East". That is the context in which we in Newfoundland receive this flawed Bill. We are not applauding.
The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. McDermid) would be very interested to know that there is a gentleman in Newfoundland, a university professor, Dr. Doug House, who wrote a book entitled "The Challenge of Oil". This gentleman is held in such high regard in Newfoundland circles, in particular by Premier Peckford and his Cabinet that they named this gentleman Chairman of the Royal Commission on Employment and Unemployment in Newfoundland. He has been travelling the province for the last year talking to Newfoundland business, labour and citizens about the problems of chronically high unemployment. This gentleman has the Premier's confidence suffice it to say.
Dr. House, who obviously enjoys the confidence of the Government, and we presume he has some confidence in the people he is now serving, has identified a number of major flaws with Bill C-94 and the Atlantic Accord. He points out the absence of any participation by Governments in the sharing of revenues. Section 40 of the accord refers to the Crown share which would be shared equitably with Newfoundland. Of course, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and her Parliamentary Secretary have subsequently eliminated
the Crown share. Newfoundland's share in Dr. House's terms ends up being "Fifty per cent of nothing."
Dr. House points out the absence of adequate provisions for a downstream processing industries, refining and petrochemicals. Under Clause 41 of the proposed legislation Newfoundland's ability to get access to crude from Hibernia is extremely questionable in the very best of circumstances.
Dr. House points out that the commitment by companies operating offshore Newfoundland, if and when that ever happens, to conduct research and development, education and training in Newfoundland is weak. In his view, the province and the federal Government, in particular the Newfoundland Government should have sought more control over this vital area because of its tremendous potential for jobs downstream.
Those are not my words, Mr. Speaker. Those are not the partisan words of one who wants to find fault for the sake of finding fault. Those are the words of the Chairman of the Royal Commission on Employment and Unemployment in Newfoundland, a gentleman who I believe has been given a formidable task, one that requires a rare amount of courage and who enjoys the confidence of the Premier who did not negotiate but was forced to sign this deal, a Premier who was told: "take it or leave it".

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: CANADA-NEWFOUNDLAND ATLANTIC ACCORD IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: You don't force Brian Peckford to do anything.

speechtext:
I will make a prediction. The same Premier who was brow beaten into taking this deal because it was the only one available just before an election when he needed something positive to announce is the same man who is saying today in Newfoundland that the Newfoundland railway shall not close. Mark my words, Mr. Speaker, before the conclusion of this session of this House at the end of June the Government of Canada will be announcing with the agreement of the Premier of Newfoundland the closure of the Newfoundland railway. It is the same Premier who said that factory freezer trawlers are a blight on the fishery of Atlantic Canada, who lamented the subsequent decision to allow factory freezer trawlers which destroyed the inshore fishery in Atlantic Canada.
I ask one thing in conclusion, Mr. Speaker. I recognize that despite the flawed nature of this Bill the Government will use its majority here and the Government will use its majority in Newfoundland to pass it. I simply beg, "Do not entrench in the Constitution this flawed, flawed and short-sighted document".

subtopic: CANADA-NEWFOUNDLAND ATLANTIC ACCORD IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, does the Liberal Party believe that the Atlantic Accord should not haved passed? Is it the policy of the Liberal Party that we should go back to the situation where the Government of Canada, in the court decisions, had complete control of the offshore resource and whatever Newfoundland got was by grace of the Government of Canada and had no rights in that offshore? Is it the Member's view that the Liberal Party would like us to go back to the position prior to the Atlantic Accord?
May 26, 1986

subtopic: CANADA-NEWFOUNDLAND ATLANTIC ACCORD IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
I am delighted the Hon. Member has asked the question, Mr. Speaker. It is obvious that he has not read the Bill. I would like to help him be more conversant. First, a brief history lesson for the Hon. Member. It was not the Government of Canada that initiated court action on ownership of the Newfoundland offshore. It was the Government of Newfoundland which began by referring the matter to the Supreme Court in Newfoundland asking, in the Premier's words, "Our court"-as if a court were political-to rule on "our ownership" of the offshore. "Our court" much to the chagrin of the Premier said no. "Our court" said Ottawa owns, the people of Canada own the offshore.
The second history lesson for the Hon. Member is that since we did not initiate the court action, the Liberal Government never took as a policy the notion that total control and ownership belonged to Ottawa and Ottawa only. We were attempting to negotiate a joint agreement. What we have ended up with is a Bill that gives ownership to Ottawa which the Hon. Member somehow suggests is terrible, and to the people of Canada, a Bill which gives Newfoundland as yet an unknown share of the revenues.
I would simply tell the Hon. Member that I find his sentiments, providing they were properly placed and supported by historical fact, interesting. I find them somewhat supportive but history will not bear out the scenario the Member has supplied. I hope I have been of some value to the Member in making him a better Member of Parliament, in giving him more understanding of that great Province of Newfoundland and in giving him more understanding of the contribution of the last Liberal Government.

subtopic: CANADA-NEWFOUNDLAND ATLANTIC ACCORD IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: We had the contribution of the last Liberal Government, Mr. Speaker, and we continue to get the contributions of this Member who continues to twist and turn and twist and turn. He is the greatest twister and turner in this House.

subtopic: CANADA-NEWFOUNDLAND ATLANTIC ACCORD IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: No, but he is close.

subtopic: CANADA-NEWFOUNDLAND ATLANTIC ACCORD IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
It is clear that the Member does not understand his own history or at least he changes his own history to suit his own facts as he needs his facts changed. The fact is the Government that he supported fought hammer and tongs to make sure that Newfoundland lost that court case in the Supreme Court of Canada. The Government could have walked away from the court case and given the rights to Newfoundland but the Government didn't. We had to have an Atlantic Accord. We had to make a deal to give Newfoundland the rights it should have. After the court case, we could not, without a constitutional amendment, change the terms, so we had to give Newfoundland all the rights and privileges which the resources in that 200 mile limit have. Does the Member and his Party want to take that away from Newfoundland? Is the Member going to vote against the Bill? Is he going to say: Newfoundland, you cannot have it; that belongs to the people of Canada and you shall not own it, you shall not
Atlantic Accord
enjoy it? Is that the way he wants to represent his province? Strange, Sir. Strange.

subtopic: CANADA-NEWFOUNDLAND ATLANTIC ACCORD IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, when I was a young boy my mother always told me that if you are going to get in these little spats out in the school yard be sure it is an even match. I feel somewhat guilty doing battle with an unarmed man.

subtopic: CANADA-NEWFOUNDLAND ATLANTIC ACCORD IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: So speaks the intellectual giant of the House of Commons.

subtopic: CANADA-NEWFOUNDLAND ATLANTIC ACCORD IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Not an intellectual giant but one who is concerned about the issues affecting his province, and one who makes sure he does his homework before he rises to spew forth, like an unguided missle, all kinds of irrelevant comments.
The Hon. Member says we could have walked away from the court case. Why did we not give it to Newfoundland? He says that in the face of a Bill from his Government which entrenches ownership of the offshore not for Newfoundland but for the Government of Canada. Can you imagine?

subtopic: CANADA-NEWFOUNDLAND ATLANTIC ACCORD IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Incredible.

subtopic: CANADA-NEWFOUNDLAND ATLANTIC ACCORD IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Incredible. You should have walked away, you nasty Liberals. Meanwhile we are debating a Bill which gives ownership not to Newfoundland but to the Government of Canada. I think that is right. I think most Newfoundlanders think that is right because they are Canadians and damned proud of it.
Let me deal with another of the foolish statements the Hon. Member made. He asked if I was going to vote against this Bill and, in doing so, take away Newfoundland's ownership of the offshore and the revenues that flow from it. The fact of the matter is that in voting for this Bill I would be voting for taking away the ownership of the offshore from Newfoundland, because in this Bill ownership is federal. In voting for this Bill I would be voting not to give Newfoundland all the revenue, because in this Bill all the revenues do not belong to Newfoundland. The majority of them are probably going to Ottawa.

speechtext: I say to the Hon. Member quite honestly that I suspect that somewhere between that confused tangle web of facts that he weaves there are some good intentions. Good luck next time out.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the issue of which the Hon. Member speaks is of course the same issue which has dominated Nova Scotia's resource development since the early 1960s. It was Robert Stanfield who raised this issue as a Premier at a constitutional conference in 1963. Successive Liberal Governments rejected the policy of the Conservative Party which was to give control of offshore resources to the coastal provinces. That was not a simple symbolic gesture by this Party. It was recognition that control of offshore resources represented an

May 26, 1986
Atlantic Accord
opportunity for the coastal provinces to take their economic place in this country. Successive Liberal Members of Parliament from Nova Scotia and Newfoundland stood idly by or sat silently in their seats in the House of Commons while successive Liberal Prime Ministers said, no, you shall remain on the welfare rolls. At the same time that gas was and is being taken from Lake Erie and other international waterways, we in Nova Scotia and Newfoundland are told, no, you are not good enough to get the same rates.
Will the Hon. Member dispute the fact that the question of offshore jurisdiction was put at issue by the federal Government in a labour arbitration case and it was subsequently decided by the Supreme Court of Canada as a constitutional decision and not subject to change by the House of Commons?

subtopic: CANADA-NEWFOUNDLAND ATLANTIC ACCORD IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find it absolutely amazing that a Member from Nova Scotia would enter this fray. Again we have a gentleman who, without understanding the risk at which he puts himself, stands and talks about how successive Liberal Governments were so nasty to the provinces. He conveniently forgets that the Premier of Nova Scotia, Mr. Buchanan, signed an offshore oil and gas development agreement with the Prime Minister of Canada, Pierre Elliott Trudeau. The last time I looked he was a Liberal. How can the Hon. Member stand up and talk about successive Liberal Governments being impossible, and then in the same breath acknowledge that the former, current, but perhaps not future, Premier of his province signed a deal with a Liberal Government? That is beyond comprehension.
Let me ask the Hon. Member a question. I heard the Hon. Member for Bonavista-Trinity-Conception (Mr. Johnson) saying that we in Newfoundland held out, fought hard and got Bill C-94 as a reward. We did not sell out like Nova Scotia. Does the Hon. Member agree with his Conservative colleague that the Premier of Nova Scotia sold out Nova Scotians when he signed the deal with the big bad, nasty and mean Liberal Government?

subtopic: CANADA-NEWFOUNDLAND ATLANTIC ACCORD IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Yes. If you look at the deal, you would think so.

subtopic: CANADA-NEWFOUNDLAND ATLANTIC ACCORD IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: I was hoping the Hon. Member would ask that question. It is obvious his research is incomplete. The offshore agreement with Nova Scotia provides that if a so-called better agreement is reached with another province, then the Premier of Nova Scotia and his Conservative Government, which will continue in office for some time, shall have the option to assume that better agreement. We have the best of both worlds. We have had development and now we are going to get any better deal on the table.

subtopic: CANADA-NEWFOUNDLAND ATLANTIC ACCORD IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wanted to say a few words about the Atlantic Accord. There is no doubt that we recall very vividly the relationship which developed between the provinces and the federal Government,
specifically between the leadership of Pierre Elliott Trudeau and the provinces. There is no doubt in anyone's mind that the relationships were extremely exacerbated. There was no feeling of co-operative federalism. There was no sense of working together. There was no recognition by that Liberal Government of the rights of the provinces with respect to their resources. We all remember the acrimonious debate between the Atlantic provinces and the federal Government over the offshore petroleum resources. The analogy was drawn that western Canada had complete control over the resources under the ground. Yet Atlantic Canada was not treated in the same way concerning those provinces' offshore resources.
There was a great deal of hope in Atlantic Canada, particularly in Newfoundland, and we in the NDP all jumped for joy when oil and gas was discovered off the coast of Newfoundland. We all hailed that as the avenue for Newfoundland to become self-supporting. As a matter of fact, we were reminded that in the not so distant past Alberta lived on the dispensation of the federal Government. It depended almost entirely on transfer payments. That is the same situation Newfoundland finds itself in today. As I said, we were all very optimistic about those resources because they seemed to be the key to Newfoundland becoming self-sustaining and independent of the federal hand-out which we call the transfer payment. Unfortunately, the Government of Canada at that time, the Trudeau Government, got into a jurisdictional dispute with the Premier and the Government of Newfoundland.

subtopic: CANADA-NEWFOUNDLAND ATLANTIC ACCORD IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: All by himself?

subtopic: CANADA-NEWFOUNDLAND ATLANTIC ACCORD IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Pardon?

subtopic: CANADA-NEWFOUNDLAND ATLANTIC ACCORD IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Peckford was not part of the dispute?

subtopic: CANADA-NEWFOUNDLAND ATLANTIC ACCORD IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
The federal Government said it owned the resources and the provinces said no, they are provincial resources. That was the dispute. We in the NDP said those resources belong to the province. We recognized that in our 1979 convention when we passed a federal resolution which became the policy of the NDP. We recognized that the provinces should have offshore jurisdiction. There was no hesitation to support the Clark Government and the Mulroney Government in recognizing that those resources belong to Newfoundland.
We agree with the general principle of this Bill. It recognizes the need for genuine provincial involvement in the exploitation of the Newfoundland offshore. Having said that, we are now into a new ball game. We have a situation where world oil prices have plummeted. Newfoundland is incapable of proceeding with respect to developing those offshore resources. Well, the Member shakes his head. In fact, the price of petroleum has dropped. What is the incentive for any development to take place if the world price for oil is between $11 and $12 U.S. a barrel and it is going to cost you $15 to $22 to produce it?
May 26, 1986

We recognize that. We socialists have no problem recognizing that since the province is entitled to develop, the province has a right to those resources, and it is the responsibility of the central Government to help the province.
Therefore, the question has to be raised, what specifically is the federal Government doing to assist Newfoundland? Nothing. We know it is withdrawing the Petroleum Incentive Program. Nothing. The PIP program has been withdrawn in the previous Bill. Nothing is being done now.
The Atlantic Accord becomes an empty shell. It is as hollow as bamboo. It has all of these sub-titles which have no meaning at all: "Joint Management", sub-heading, "Decisions In Relation To Offshore Management". It covers "Suspense Of Vetos", "Ministerial Directives", "Public Review Pricing", "Revenue Sharing". Revenue sharing-if you have not got any revenue what are you going to share? All of those impressive sub-titles in this Accord mean absolutely nothing.
The offshore activity has died over the last year. This Conservative Government has done nothing to restore that activity, nothing whatsoever. The need for some decisive action on the part of the federal Government is quite clear. What has it brought before Parliament? It has brought before Parliament an Accord that offers nothing specifically to Newfoundland, not a thing. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. McDermid) shakes his head. I wish that he could point out specifically in this Accord what it is that the federal Government intends to do to assist Newfoundland to develop the offshore.
The hopes were high, and there is a considerable investment already in the infrastructure surrounding the offshore resource, but unfortunately with the downturn in price nothing is happening.
Even the newspapers in Canada recognize the problem. The local paper from Newfoundland, the Halifax Chronicle-Herald, points out that last week in Newfoundland-and this was dated April 30, 1986-organizations representing 700 companies told reporters that spending on offshore exploration would plummet to $100 million in 1987. Both companies, Mobil and Chevron have already announced major cut-backs in exploration expenditures in 1986 and both carry heavy debt loads.
In light of that, what is the federal Government doing? No one could say now that there is acrimony between the leadership of the federal Government and the leadership in the provincial Government. They both belong to the same political Party.

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of State (Finance)) moved
subtopic: DUTIES RELIEF ACT
speechtext:
that Bill C-98, an Act to consolidate various enactments that provide for drawbacks, reductions, refunds and remissions of duties, other than export drawbacks for which provision is made in Sections 82 to 87 of the Customs Act, to amend the customs tariff and to repeal or revoke the enactments so consolidated, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
She said: Mr. Speaker, first, I should apologize to the House for the length of the title of this Bill and its cumbersome and undescriptive nature. However, it is a very important Bill and I am very pleased to introduce it in the House today. This legislation, to be known as the Duties Relief Act, provides for reductions or removal of duties and excise taxes under certain conditions. The Bill is based on a Ways and Means motion tabled as part of the Budget of May 23, 1985.
Before proceeding to outline the provisions of the Bill, it might be helpful if I indicated the context in which these measures have been developed over some considerable time.

The imposing of customs duties on goods imported into Canada is an important tool of our trade policy. One of the objectives of the customs tariff has always been to promote investment, production and thus employment in Canada. The Tariff gives Canadian manufacturers the benefit of a cost advantage, which helps them compete with goods that are similar to or substitutes for the products they manufacture.
There are cases, however, when it may be inappropriate for Canadian manufacturers to pay duty on their imports. In recent years, after consultations with Canadian industry, a number of programs were set up when it was found desirable to grant a remission of duty to certain manufacturers, subject to certain conditions.
The proposed legislation will bring together, in one statute, sections from other Acts as well as various regulations, all of which provide for duty relief programs of considerable benefit to Canadians in manufacturing and other industries. Although the individual measures have been in force for some years, this is the first time they have been incorporated into a single piece of legislation.
To be able to make effective use of these measures, which until now appeared in a variety of legislative instruments, required considerable time and effort by companies to ferret out just what the provisions were and to determine whether they were applicable to their particular circumstances. While the experts knew where to look, business people without this expertise were at a distinct disadvantage. Similarly, those seeking to package the federal Government's programs found the current system difficult to utilize.

This initiative is in line with the Government's commitment to make its services easier to understand and use. The proposed legislation will be easier to administer and will help Canadian companies use the provisions respecting custom duty and excise tax to better advantage. In this respect, it should be well received by local and provincial Governments, especially British Columbia which has asked for these customs procedures to be adopted so that it can attract new investment.

I would now like to turn for a few moments to the clauses of the Bill itself which take account of differing circumstances. Clause 4 provides authority for the Governor in Council on the recommendation of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) to reduce or remove duties on materials, at the time of their importation, to be used in Canadian manufactures. This authority has been used on many occasions to allow manufacturers to import materials not available from Canadian sources at reduced rates of duty in order to better meet import competition.
Under Clauses 5 to 8, duty is refunded only after the imported goods have been used for the purposes specified.
Clauses 9 to 15 provide for the inclusion of the machinery program in the Bill without any change in the scope of the program. However, there will be a streamlining of procedures which will implement a recommendation of the ministerial Task Force on Program Review tabled with the May, 1985 Budget to reduce the paper-burden and delays.
May 26, 1986

The machinery program, which has been in effect since January, 1968, serves the needs of users and manufacturers of machinery. It provides for the remission of duty on machinery which falls under the program and which is not available from Canadian production. It also ensures that Canadian manufacturers receive the protection provided by the statutory rates in the customs tariff as soon as they can demonstrate a capability to produce the relevant machinery. The criteria for determining availability are set out in the Bill.
Under the current procedure, duties are remitted by Order in Council on a weekly basis. Under the procedure proposed in the Bill, the Minister of National Revenue would publish a list of "not available" and "available" machinery. Such a list will significantly reduce the present requirement for the processing of thousands of applications under the program. Relief will be granted immediately on goods at the time of their importation simply by reference to the "not available" list. Consequently, it will not be necessary, other than in exceptional circumstances, to submit and process specific applications. As a result there will be fewer cases of companies paying duty and then claiming a refund.
Clauses 16 to 19 of the Bill allow processors to obtain relief from duties on goods which are brought into Canada for processing and then exported, if certain conditions are complied with. This means that Canadian firms do not have to tie up large sums of money in duty for long periods of time, which, of course, adds to their costs and makes their products less competitive abroad.
Clauses 24 to 28 permit Canadian firms to send goods outside Canada for repair, to have equipment added or to be further processed and to pay duty only on the value of the work done abroad. One of the conditions to be met is that this work could not have been done in Canada.
The other specific provision I would like to mention at this time is one which corresponds to a section of the Financial Administration Act. Under Section 17 of that Act, the Governor in Council may remit any tax, fee or penalty. In addition to some of the programs I have mentioned earlier, this authority has been used to help such industries as manufacturers of construction equipment and of semi-conductors. It is proposed that there be a separate authority-Clause 37-to deal specifically with the remission of duties and excise taxes.
In summary, I think Hon. Members will appreciate that the new legislation will be beneficial to Canadians and Canadian companies. It will be less difficult to administer and it should encourage Canadian companies to take full advantage of the duty and excise tax provisions which are there for their benefit. It will also be of considerable use to all levels of Government and, I think, to the private sector, as we approach people who want to invest in Canada in order to make this a favourable country in which to invest.
Finally, what I am proposing today is very much in keeping with our philosophy and the commitment of the Government to make our services to business and to the public easier to use,
Duties Relief Act
easier to understand and more beneficial in terms of the operation of the country.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make it clear to the House today that although we agree with the principle of this Bill, we must get the message across to Canadians that we can't afford to let everything go and lose control, and that while it is a good thing to try and simplify the administration of our customs legislation, it is also very important to exercise a certain degree of control.
Before I finish, Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out that there is a provision in this legislation that the Department of National Revenue may establish a list of the machinery and equipment produced in Canada and a list of the machinery and equipment that is not. I think we should remember there are many small companies that manufacture machinery and equipment and often cannot afford to advertise. I therefore hope the Department will find a way to ensure that our small manufacturing companies will not be penalized and that every importer of machinery and equipment will have a complete list so that he can check whether certain types of equipment or machinery are already being manufactured in this country.

subtopic: DUTIES RELIEF ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, much of this Bill is certainly not very controversial and I doubt the House will spend much time debating the measures of Bill C-
98. In essence, the Government wishes to clean up some of the various regulations that exist.
There are some things, not in terms of specifics but in terms of philosophy and motivation behind Bill C-98, with which I do have some concerns. I suspect that the Bill paves the way for free trade zones. There is much in this Bill that would address the various problems that would have to be overcome if we were to establish free trade zones in Canada.
In the past, the Province of British Columbia passed Bill 49 entitled the Special Enterprise Zones and Tax Relief Act, offering special tax status to corporations investing in such zones and surrounding communities. The foundation of much of the thinking of the Bennett Government on free enterprise zones originates with the influential Fraser Institute, the institute that has been advocating free trade zones.
In free trade zones, the normal labour and environmental legislation often does not exist. According to the people who have conceived of free trade zones, and particularly those from the Fraser Institute, a free trade zone is a little geographic space that is thrown back into the 18th or 19th century. Normal tax laws, social policies, labour legislation, environmental protection legislation and all the more modern laws no longer have effect. This allows raw capitalism to operate without any hindrance in these particular areas.
We can see by reading the various clauses in this legislation that the Bill comes very close to paving the way for free trade zones. For example, in 1983, an External Affairs paper entitled A Review of Canadian Trade Policy contained the following statement:
Canada does not have free-trade zones but it does have a number of tariff policy instruments which achieve essentially the same objectives.
The two programs referred to were the inward processing remission order, and the various temporary tariff items which provide duty-free entry for specific components required in Canadian manufacturing. Indeed, the legislation before us today puts together the various bits and pieces of rules and regulations so that they form a more orderly pattern, thus allowing for the introduction of free trade zones somewhere down the line.
We are also concerned with the general direction being taken by Customs and Excise. I know that this is not directly related to Bill C-98, but I will take this opportunity to raise this matter in the House of Commons today. We are afraid that the various measures the Government has taken in the name of saving taxpayers' money has degraded the level of service provided by Customs in Canada. For instance, no longer are Customs officers looking at individual pieces of mail and parcels that come into Canada. Rather, these parcels of imported goods are sent directly to the recipients without being inspected by Customs officers. The recipients are then required to go voluntarily to Customs to make their declarations and to pay whatever duties are necessary. This method is being undertaken on a trial basis in Montreal and the figures show that the estimated loss of revenue caused by this new practice
May 26, 1986

is far greater than the cost to the Government of employing the various Customs officers.
At the Toronto airport, management decided to allow all sorts of imported goods to be released from bonded warehouses without proper inspection and paperwork. About a month ago,
I had the opportunity to tour the Customs facility at the Toronto airport. That facility is one of the largest such facilities in Canada and certainly the Toronto airport is the busiest when it comes to receiving goods into Canada. Customs officers at that airport face very bleak working conditions. There is very little natural light. There are rows and rows of computers, a very inhuman working environment. The employees are required to process mountains of paper every day. Sometimes a computer spits out a particular invoice or entry form because it has not been filled out properly. The goods involved are in the country and are released from the bonded warehouse, but the paperwork still has to be corrected. Perhaps a wrong tariff item was used or some paperwork did not quite fit in. A few months ago a pile of paperwork had accumulated, with entry forms which were improperly filled out or whatever, and management decided to release all the goods. It decided not to figure out the individual items or the incorrect entries. It more or less decided to forgive the whole batch, and we really do not know how much it has cost Canadian taxpayers.
If one's import forms are incorrectly filled out and they end up on top of the big pile with which Customs can no longer deal, it certainly appears that Customs will look the other way. In other words, it appears that there will be one law for one individual and another law for another; it depends upon the draw, so to speak.
Certainly the cut-backs which have affected the Customs Department have resulted in there being demoralized Customs officers across the country. Canada can be proud of the job which the Customs and Excise has done. From speaking with Customs officers at various points across the country, I can tell Hon. Members that the morale is very low. They feel they do not have the ability nor the resources to enforce Canadian law.
I should like to draw the attention of Hon. Members to the fact that other serious problems exist in our Customs Inspection Branch. They have to deal with so much paper every day that very often they do not have the opportunity of properly inspecting and being on top of what is coming into the country. Certainly my office and I are looking into instances in which illegal automatic guns and weapons have been coming through Customs without proper inspection. There is no one in Customs, certainly not in the Toronto airport, who is an expert on guns and knows which guns can or cannot be allowed into the country. Most Customs officers have to deal with a mountain of paper every day. Therefore, very few of the cases of automatic and semi-automatic weapons being imported into Canada are receiving proper inspection. I draw this matter to
Duties Relief Act
the attention of the House because it is another indication of the serious problems in Customs and Excise today.
I urge the Government to take heed of my remarks this afternoon and to understand that there are some serious problems. Hopefully it will back away from its gung-ho approach to cutting back on the resources of Customs and Excise. I hope the Government gives it proper study and indeed determines the cost effectiveness of sending out parcels to individual importers without them being expected by Customs people. It should also study the loss of public revenue which this entails and compare it with what it would cost to pay the salaries of some extra Customs officers.
I ask it to take heed of the situation at Toronto airport where the staff has not been increased over the last number of years. However, the traffic coming through that airport has dramatically increased, so we find individual Customs officers are totally overworked and do not have the expertise they require to deal with items such as automatic weapons and other weapons which could prove to be illegal. As I said, I hope the Government heeds my warning this afternoon and takes a closer look at what it is doing to our Customs officers, those men and women who are required to uphold Canadian laws.
I have no immediate objection to Bill C-98, other than my concern that its motivation is to help set up free trade zones in the country. Certainly we in the New Democratic Party will oppose that move. We do not believe that Canada can solve its economic problems by returning to a 19th century model. Canada's economic strength and well-being lie in people being able to work and to receive decent wages from that work, so that they have the power to purchase the goods and services which they need to live good and decent lives. Certainly cheap labour in free trade zones will not help Canada in achieving its goal of economic prosperity for all.

PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS HIGH INTEREST RATES CHARGED ON CREDIT CARDS
speechtext:
That the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs be empowered to study the question of excessively high interest rates charged by the issuers of credit cards and charge cards.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to debate this motion. It is true that under the new rules governing the House a committee now has the power to initiate such investigations, which was not the case when the motion was written. It is still relevant for the House to give direction to its committees, which are extensions of the House. It is true that the committee can carry out this mandate with much more enthusiasm and commitment knowing that it has the authority of the House behind it.
I have submitted this motion to the House and I hope it will receive support from all quarters. It concerns a major consumer problem. Two-thirds of the adults of Canada now use credit cards. The average adult has three of these cards. About 40 per cent of credit card users pay interest charges. Are they receiving justice? I put the question to you, Mr. Speaker, that while interest rates affecting consumers and investors have gone up and down in the main, interest rates on charge cards and credit cards have not. The bank rate goes up and down but the interest rate on credit and charge cards remains the same year after year. For example, MasterCard issuers, such as the Bank of Montreal, the National Bank, the Victoria and Grey Trust, raised their interest charges a few years ago to 21 per cent when the bank rate was very high. Since then the bank rate has come down but the charges to consumers have not. Canada Trust charges 18.45 per cent. The Royal Trust began issuing its MasterCard last fall with a discount rate of 14 per cent. This rate has now been raised to 14.75 per cent yet in the same period of time the bank rate has fallen.
Are those rates too high? That question has already been answered by a competitor of MasterCard, namely VISA. It has issued ads which said, "Are you fed up with paying high interest rates on your MasterCard accounts?" The industry has put the question which I have raised before the House today. Obviously charges are too high.
We must also ask the question to issuers of VISA cards. In addition to an annual or a transaction fee, VISA charges now range from a low of 15.9 per cent to 18.6 per cent by four banks, the Bank of Nova Scotia, the Bank of Commerce, the Royal Bank, and the Toronto Dominion, in spite of the fact that the bank rate has come down. It is not only the issuers of MasterCard and VISA that are imposing charges far above what is justified by the rate issuers have to pay for the money they use, but gasoline credit card charges are much higher still. Companies such as Sunoco, Imperial, Texaco, Shell and Gulf as well as PetroCan-which used to say "It's ours"-now

I believe the banks are charging interest, not service charges. Their service charges are covered by the merchants. Member when he says that MasterCard charges 21 per cent. VISA charges

We know interest rates have gone down, so how much handling charges can they have? Talking about handling charges, if it costs so much, how come the banks are advertising so much? How come the banks encourage people to use their cards?
If memory serves me right, when credit cards were instituted you used to pay a fee. Some respected credit card companies still charge a serious fee. Every month you get a statement you have to pay the full amount. There is no question of deferring your payment. VISA and MasterCard tell you on your statement that the minimum payment is $10 or whatever. You can pay that and they charge you interest on the balance. We are not dealing here with just a credit card, it is a personal loan. Everyone with a credit card has a line of credit. You can buy whatever you want and at the end of the month you can pay in full. They do not charge you interest if you pay in full because they are getting handling charges from the merchant. That is why I say it is an interest charge and not a service charge. If you pay at the end of the month there is no interest. They are collecting a service charge from the merchant. However, if you only make a partial payment, they charge you interest.
I think the banks are taking advantage of this credit line they created for consumers. It gives them a lot of business. Just consider the number of credit cards issued. Practically everyone today, including myself, use credit cards. However, when people borrow money, business people or whoever, they do not have to pay interest rates like that. Why should the consumer have to pay those interest rates?
I agree that the Government should look into this. The Minister said he is looking into it, but he is off on the wrong foot because he believes that the interest rate includes service charges. That is not the case. I repeat, service charges are paid by the merchant.

However, I have to say to the Member that he was lecturing the wrong people. I do not think there is a single Member of this House who will defend the banks or the oil companies or
the department stores, all of whom are ripping off the customers who do not pay their monthly accounts immediately. The people who refused to take any action when this was raised by Members of Parliament are the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Cote), the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDou-gall). When they were asked about this, their response was that, first, they are quite prepared to leave it to the market to decide what interest rates should be. As well, without any investigation or question, they adopt the defence of these companies that they are not overcharging. There is no investigation by the Ministers concerned or their Departments. That is why I say that the Hon. Member has brought this question to the wrong place.
Last November 20, when interest rates came down again, we asked the Conservative Government, when it was boasting about low interest rates, low interest rates for whom? We pointed out what was happening to people who do not pay their outstanding bills immediately. They had no answer. There was no action. I point out to Members of the House that there are 16 million credit card holders in Canada, half of whom pay off their balances each month and do not pay any interest. Who are they? They are people in the middle and upper-income brackets. I am sure there is not a Member of Parliament who does not pay his or her account every month without being charged interest. That leaves 8 million people who pay 18 per cent to 21 per cent interest if they do not pay up at the end of the month. They pay 24 per cent for an oil company credit card and 28 per cent for a department store credit card. The Hon. Member gives some credit to VISA. I understand that VISA charges a service charge, a dollar a month whether you use it or not.

If the Hon. Member is going to give credit to VISA, we better see what that adds up to.
Let us look at the reality. These rates have not essentially changed for consumers since September, 1984, when the Conservative Government, of which the Hon. Member for Scarborough West is a Member, took office. From September, 1984 until today interest rates have dropped from 12.28 per cent to 8.43 per cent. These robbers are still charging the same rates they established in 1981 when prime money rates were well over 20 per cent. What has the Government said about this? Members, including the Member for Scarborough West, have asked the Government, and both the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Cote) say they will not interfere with the market. The market magic will fix everything. What has it fixed?

The market has provided us with gold cards at $75 a year, great for high-income earners who pay off their bills every month. The market has allowed organized retailers to cut their costs in retailing with credit cards by reducing the charge to
May 26, 1986

the retailers for using cards to less than 2 per cent. They have not passed that on to the consumers. Consumers have not received anything in the way of reduction, even though the New York Federal Reserve Bank in the United States calls this type of financial dealing "the single most profitable of all loans made by major banks". Of course, they are individuals, they are people in the lower income brackets and they have no political clout. So the American and Canadian Governments have let them get away with it.
The question which we should ask is, what would the Government have done differently if it really wanted to ensure that consumers receive a fair share of the lower interest rate on their charge card purchases? This is the kind of question the Member for Scarborough West should ask his Minister. It could have investigated thoroughly whether the costs of operating the charge cards are as high as the banks say they are. The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs just took their statement that they were not overcharging as gospel truth and refused to do anything about it.
Our information is that about half of the charge card costs are administrative and half are for the cost of money. If the cost of money has declined, as we know, and as every Conservative Member wants us to know, because of the great policies of that Government, if they declined by 3.85 per cent from September until now, then the card holders could have had the interest rate reduced by 2 per cent, because that is half of the reduction in the interest rate. That would have saved the bank credit card holders over $100 million a year. If you add to that the overcharging by the trust companies, the oil companies and the department stores, we are talking of probably close to $200 million. We are talking about huge amounts of money, and the Government has been quite content to take the credit card companies' word that they are not making much money, or that the market will somehow work in the consumer's favour. Second, the Government, if it felt that consumers' interests were being sacrificed to those of almost everybody else, could have acted on the consumers' behalf and begun a rigorous examination of consumer credit and sought some legislative relief. We do not need another study. That is again just putting off dealing with this very serious problem.
One solution which we favour, and which the Government should be looking at, is a ceiling rate for credit card interest, which would show that the market is sensitive as interest rates come down or go up. An interest rate ceiling on cards pegged to the amount that banks actually pay for their money would be very helpful.
We ought to have heard from the Government some sound consumer advice about the cost of credit. We should not be saying that the market will decide, when the market is rigged against the poor consumer. There has been a real rip-off of hundreds of millions of dollars which the Government has permitted. We should be urging consumers to find alternative sources of credit. We should encourage them to form credit unions of their own where they do not exist. We have begun to educate the people so they do not get ripped off too much by

the income tax discounters. Why do we not begin to educate the people who get into trouble because of buying too much and get caught in this credit card squeeze?
We will support this motion going to committee, but to us it is just another way of postponing any serious, real action on what is a disgraceful situation, the rip-off of hundreds of millions of dollars every year by the banks, by the oil companies and by the department stores. I know it probably comes as a great satisfaction to him today to hear Members from all Parties address this matter in a non-partisan fashion. I think there is certainly a feeling among all three Parties that the matter of credit card interest rates must be dealt with.
To deal specifically with interest rates, this matter has obviously come to the attention of the public after at least three to four years of great fluctuations in rates where they hit a peak bank rate approaching 20 per cent and then, of course, fluctuated from there. It has really been only in recent months, since the election of this Government, that we have seen interest rates begin to stabilize and, in fact, drop. I was very pleased to hear the Member from the New Democratic Party refer to a bank rate now under 9 per cent. This gives considerable urgency to the matter when we have a bank rate at 8.3 per cent, and the disparity between that bank rate and credit card interest rates is probably the greatest in many years.
Dealing with the argument of a relative rate for credit cards, it is obvious that credit card rates will be higher than established loan rates, somewhat higher than the prime rate, as I think all Members agree there is an administrative cost built in.

Mr. Speaker, I also welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate on the motion moved in the House by the Hon. Member for Scarborough West (Mr. Stackhouse).

First of all, Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the Member for bringing forward this motion to our attention this afternoon. I want to draw your attention to the very important component of this motion which refers to the excessively high interest rates charged by the issuer of credit cards and charge cards. Indeed, the really important ingredient of the motion before us today is to recognize, as the Hon. Member has, that these rates are excessive and totally unacceptable. The wording of the motion sends a very clear message to the Finance Committee about the work that is required of it.
While I am not proposing an amendment, I hope the Finance Committee will take other costs into account when it studies this motion. I hope the Hon. Member will agree that the entire costs of credit cards should be studied. I am not only referring to interest rates on credit cards but also to the consumer fees that are charged in many cases. For example, one credit card company charges 25 per cent for every transaction up to a certain amount. Other credit card companies charge a fee at the beginning of the year, with no subsequent fees. A variety of fees are included in one form or another, which really add to the cost for the consumer who is purchasing a variety of goods.
The Hon. Member for Scarborough West (Mr. Stackhouse) will probably be a member of that Finance Committee and I hope he takes that suggestion into account when the committee studies this matter.
I think Parliament should look into the impact that credit cards have on pricing. This refers to fees that are charged to businesses. If a retail store knows that it will have to pay 4 per cent in order to have the service of a credit card company and knows that half of its business will be conducted by credit card, obviously it will increase the price of its merchandise by 2 per cent in order to recover its cost. This represents another cost to the consumer that is not often mentioned.

Mr. Speaker, I recall going south of the border several times and in some American cities people who do not use credit cards are given discounts. For example, a gas station will offer a 2 or 3 per cent discount to customers paying cash rather than using a credit card. This is the kind of initiative they take in some American states, but so far I do not remember ever seeing the same kind of offer here in Canada. In my opinion this would be one of the main issues which should be reviewed by the parliamentary committee which will study the credit card system and the excessively high rates charged by the issuers of these cards, as our colleague from Scarborough West so clearly indicated.
To conclude very briefly, Mr. Speaker-because hopefully the motion will be adopted this afternnon and be considered by the parliamentary committee which deals with financial matters-I would like to echo my other colleagues in commending the Hon. Member for Scarborough West for bringing this motion before the House today and suggesting that the question of excessively high interest rates charged by the issuers of credit cards be considered. Indeed we hope that the fact that we are debating this issue in the House today might encourage the issuers of credit cards to lower their interest charges. In my judgment it does not make any sense at all that banks can lend money at 12 or 13 per cent, and yet issuers of credit cards charge 18, 21 or 24 per cent. Worse still, some department stores charge 28 per cent to finance the cost of the products they sell.
As we know, a less enlightened consumer will often be tempted to use a credit card instead of borrowing from a bank or trust company. I would suggest this may be too convenient a way for him to buy what he wants, but later on he realizes that his purchase is financed at these excessively high rates. I believe it should be hoped that all consumers would use their credit cards constructively, such as using it for a month and then paying the total balance at the end of that month. But, unfortunately, the economic condition of some of our constituents are such that often when they need something, they use their credit cards to purchase it and unhappily cannot afford to pay in due time. For those people especially, we should do what we can to reduce interest rates, as suggested by our colleague, the Hon. Member for Scarborough West.
It is therefore my hope that when we do consider the matter, we will be looking not only at interest rates as suggested by the Hon. Member, but also at the impact on prices that the whole credit card system has, and finally indirect costs. I am referring to the monthly charges or the once-a-year fee

subtopic: OFFICIAL LANGUAGES-SUPREME COURT DECISIONS-REQUEST FOR INTRODUCTION OF CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT. (B) FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE AGENDA

speechtext:
Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, on May 1 the Supreme Court of Canada rendered three judgments on minority language rights which, regretfully, cut back on what were perceived to be, and in some jurisdictions this was the practice over the years, constitutionally entrenched rights. These judgments dealt with cases originating in Quebec, Manitoba and New Brunswick.
In the Quebec case, Duncan MacDonald, a Quebec Anglophone, argued that by virtue of Article 133 of the Constitution of 1867, he had the right to a court summons in the English language, whereas he had been summoned to court by the City of Montreal in the French language only.
Unfortunately, the Supreme Court ruled that Article 133 gave the state, that is the city, a province or the federal Government, and in this case the City of Montreal, the right to choose the language of summons before a federal or Quebec court, and not the citizen called to answer before the court.
This is a regrettable and illogical judgment. Surely the rights entrenched in Section 133 of the Constitution, which allow for the use of French or English before the courts, are to benefit individuals and not the state. When I asked the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) about this matter on May 5, and in particular whether he would propose a constitutional amendment to fill the gap left by the Supreme Court judgments, he answered, first of all, that no rights were lost by these judgments, which is absolutely ridiculous. Everyone that I have met and read on those judgments agreed that rights were lost, including the Commissioner of Official Languages.
Second, he answered that he would propose ordinary legislation to deal with the situation, but not constitutional amendments. Ordinary laws are not enough because they can easily be changed and do not prevail over other legislation. They do not provide for entrenched rights. I am not surprised by the attitude taken by the Minister.
When the MacDonald case was being argued before the Supreme Court of Canada in December of 1984, his Department argued, in a factum that he signed, the very position that
the court adopted on May 1, 1986, a few weeks ago, namely that Duncan MacDonald did not have the right to a summons in English.
This not only represents narrow bureaucratic thinking on the part of the Minister and the Government, but it is a very offhanded way of dealing with entrenched language rights, which are supposed to help ordinary citizens. It is also another broken promise by the Conservative Party, in this case made to the official language groups and minorities in Canada, that their language rights would be protected.
Once again tonight I ask the Minister of Justice or his Parliamentary Secretary, who is here representing him, to use good, common, political sense and to propose a constitutional amendment which will truly guarantee these important rights to our language minorities.
Mr. Chris Speyer (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of
Justice): Mr. Speaker, let me state immediately that the federal Government is deeply committed to greater protection for official languages in the area of the administration of justice that goes beyond the minimum constitutional requirement regarding the use of English or French before the courts. The progressive official languages policy of this Government is based on ongoing improvements in this indispensable area of our national life.
As the Hon. Member knows, the Government expects to bring forward, before the end of the year, new legislation to revise the Official Languages Act. We are working on proposed amendments that will not only ensure that this Act is in full compliance with the Constitution, but will strengthen and enhance language rights so that this vital piece of legislation truly reflects our progressive policy.
The Hon. Member can rest assured that we intend to fully address the questions that were in issue in the Supreme Court case to which he has alluded. Special care is given to measures to enhance language rights in the administration of justice and, in particular, in proceedings before federal courts and tribunals.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when we were debating in this chamber in 1980-81 the national energy policy and the PIP grant system, I recall bringing to the attention of the House the potential for abuse. If the Government is going to cover 80 per cent of the costs of the taxpayers of Canada, it is not hard to adjust the costs one way or another so that, in fact, the taxpayers end up paying just about everything.
I do not know whether this has been done in the case of Exco Energy Corporation. That matter might eventually be decided by the courts. However, last December, mainly on behalf of the creditors, I asked what was happening with
May 26, 1986

respect to the Exco fiasco and if there was going to be anything left for the creditors when the dust settled. The reply at that time was, in fact, a non-reply because the matter was under investigation by the RCMP.
It is my information that the RCMP investigation was completed some time in February. Since that time a wall of silence has descended over the whole affair and we know no more about it than we did last December.
I recall in March, 1985, talking with the PIP administration people and asking them to conduct full and complete audits of Exco Energy, formally known as Forward Resources. I believe I was in touch with them before that time because there was a common suspicion in the area in which they were operating that something was untoward. There were reports of exploration programs that cost five or six times what would be the cost for a normal, prudent operator.
Eventually-some time last year-they were not able to meet their commitments. I understand that they owe approximately $7 million in the Northwest Territories alone and considerably more than that in the Province of Alberta, and perhaps in British Columbia and Yukon. The bankruptcy of Exco has been responsible, at least in part, for a series of bankruptcies in the Northwest Territories, including Beaufort Foods, BeauTuk Marine and Buffalo Air. It is a domino effect which commonly occurs in these situations. Hardships are widespread among many people who are creditors of Exco or creditors of the creditors of Exco.
There are many unanswered questions that I hope the Parliamentary Secretary will address in his reply. First, we would like to know whether A1 Langard, one of the principals involved in Exco, is back in Canada. It was said that he had left the country, but let us hope that he is back. Did the RCMP investigations reveal any wrongdoing? The investigations are over and we have not heard anything.
Will any charges be laid in connection with Exco? Was any of the cash or other assets of Exco transferred to other corporations such as AJL Investments Ltd. immediately before the bankruptcy occurred? Did Exco make application for and collect more in the way of PIP grants than it lawfully had coming to it?
Are there any PIP grants still collectable by Exco or the trustees of Exco? That is an important question because if there is anything left for the creditors, it will probably be paid out of PIP grants that are payable to Exco. I understand that a $10 million payment was made some time last year. That was seized by the bank. The bank considered itself first on the list and took the $10 million. There was nothing left for anyone else. If there are further Government payments to Exco, will they go to the creditors or will something of a like nature happen again?
What the creditors really want to know is, as I asked in December, when the dust settles, will there be anything left for
Adjournment Debate
them at all? Those are the questions I sincerely hope the Parliamentary Secretary will be able to answer.

speakeroldname: Mr. John McDermid (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: ENERGY-EXCO ENERGY CORPORATION-PLIGHT OF CREDITORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I always enjoy the questions coming from my friend, the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson). They are very thorough. I can tell him right now that I can answer some of the questions he posed and others I cannot. It is difficult to discuss this entire matter with any degree of candidness. It is currently under RCMP investigation and the subject of a case before the Federal Court of Canada. However, I would like to make the point that the federal Government does appreciate that a number of small businesses in the Northwest Territories and Alberta are facing financial difficulties as a result of the Exco Energy case.
Many Members of the House may be aware that last year the creditors of Exco Energy Limited, or Forward Resources Limited, as it was formerly known, voted to place Exco into bankruptcy. As a consequence of this action, the affairs of the company are now in the hands of a trustee who will distribute the realizable assets of the company.
As Members of the House will also be aware, Exco trustees have just filed a suit in the Federal Court of Canada against the federal Government claiming failure to pay $26 million in PIP grants, resulting in damages of $110 million. It should be noted that concurrent with the bankruptcy proceedings, the RCMP investigation is proceeding to determine whether or not charges will be laid against the company. Naturally, we cannot comment on either the court case or the investigation.
With respect to the Petroleum Incentives Payment moneys owing to Exco, I wish to state that officials within the Petroleum Incentives Administration have been conducting an intensive audit since the spring of 1985. Well over 90 per cent of the audit has now been completed. Audit results to date indicate that no additional moneys are owed to Exco by the PIA. In fact, results would indicate that the federal Government is also a creditor of Exco.
The audits were presented to the trustee on a well-by-well and program-by-program basis as they were completed. The trustee has been invited to respond to the audit Findings prior to final decisions being taken on them. The trustee has never responded to the audit findings, although some were presented to him over six months ago, and has chosen to serve the Crown with a statement of claim in the Federal Court for $26 million in PIP incentives and $110 million in damages. The Crown filed its statement of defence on May 15, 1986.
In light of the legal action in the Federal Court, the Crown has no choice but to proceed with its claim in the bankruptcy proceedings. As the criminal investigation of the RCMP is still under way and the civil action is before the courts, I must decline comment as to the case. I am sure the Hon. Member will understand the predicament in which we find ourselves.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at least the Minister does not tend to be hypocritical. My colleague has raised a very important issue, one to which we are devoting very close attention. The Acting Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Mazankowski) is seized of this question and has been aware of it for many years, as the Hon. Member, if he appreciates the history of this Chamber, will understand. The matter has been raised in depth on a number of occasions with the unions, management and the entire marine industry in Canada. The future of our shipyards is one on which I need no lecture from the Hon. Member.
I suggest that there is no easy solution. The Government has already made an enormous contribution to the survival of this industry by providing through its own orders the great bulk of business now on the order books. It has already shown flexibility in its contractual dealings with the shipyards. For example, it agreed to renegotiate its contracts with Halifax Industries Limited so that the company could complete orders it already has with the Department of Transport for some Coast Guard vessels with ice-breaking capabilities.
The Government will continue to support the shipyards through public procurements. The Polar VIII ice-breaker program, the program to which my colleague referred, is under
Adjournment Debate
study and the patrol frigate program is under way. These two programs alone will provide some 10,000 person-years of employment to this very hard pressed industry.
To assure the future of the shipyards for the long term, they must also obtain commercial work. In the face of the collapse of world demand, coupled with the addition of new capacities in countries such as Korea, competition is fierce in all the markets of the world. We must, therefore, make sure that Canadian shipyards work at very high levels of efficiency without imposing an economic burden on the users of Canadian built ships. I am sure my colleague understands that.
For these reasons, the Government will be undertaking discussions and will be continuing discussions that are already ongoing over the course of the summer with the industry, labour and the provinces to solicit proposals for dealing with the future of the shipbuilding sector.
